full_statement:
Assume AC. Let $G_0\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be discrete and torsion-free. For any subgroup $H$, write $\Lambda_H$ for its actual hyperbolic orbit limit set and $\Omega_H=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\Lambda_H$. Supply elementary or geometrically finite subgroups $J_1,J_2\le G_0$, where geometrical finiteness means finite volume of a positive-radius neighborhood of the convex hull quotient. Supply $J_i$-invariant closed Jordan discs $B_i$, with boundaries $S_i$ and disjoint interiors $U_i$, and $f\in\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ satisfying
$$f(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus B_1)=U_2,\qquad fJ_1f^{-1}=J_2.$$
Impose the full jointly blocked conditions: $B_i\cap\Omega_{G_0}=B_i\cap\Omega_{J_i}$; the two regular parts are jointly precisely invariant, meaning
$$g(B_i\cap\Omega_{G_0})\cap(B_j\cap\Omega_{G_0})=\varnothing$$
unless $i=j$ and $g\in J_i$; and, at every rank-one parabolic point of $J_i$, in a coordinate with that point infinity and generator $z\mapsto z+\ell$, $\ell>0$, the finite part of $S_i$ lies in some strip $|\operatorname{Im}z|\le R$. There is no clearance requirement at rank-two parabolics. Assume the actual proper gap
$$A_0=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\bigcup_{g\in G_0}g(B_1\cup B_2)$$
is nonempty. Boundaries may meet, including at parabolic points with enlarged stabilizers in $G=\langle G_0,f\rangle$.

Then $G$ is the discrete torsion-free HNN extension furnished by the algebraic supplier. Each $S_i$ is a precisely embedded $(J_i,G)$ block in the following explicit sense:
$$S_i\cap\Lambda_G=\Lambda_{J_i},\qquad S_i\cap\Omega_G=S_i\cap\Omega_{J_i},$$
the latter regular set is precisely invariant under $J_i$ in $G$, and every translate $gS_i$ is contained in one of the two closed complementary discs of $S_i$. The same rank-one boundary clearance remains valid. Distinct translated boundaries have spherical diameters tending to zero. There is a sequence of pairwise disjoint translated boundaries nesting about $x$—each separates $x$ from its predecessor and their diameters and distances to $x$ tend to zero—if and only if
$$x\in\Lambda_G\setminus\bigcup_{g\in G}g\Lambda_{G_0}.$$
Every element not conjugate into $G_0$ is loxodromic or is parabolic whose fixed point, after conjugacy, is a parabolic point of $J_1$ (equivalently of a conjugate of $J_2$). No assertion of geometrical finiteness of $G$ is made.

There is also the exact conformal quotient gluing. Put
$$R=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\bigcup_{g\in G_0}g(U_1\cup U_2),\qquad Q=R\cap\Omega_{G_0}.$$
The quotient $Q/G_0$ is a possibly disconnected surface with boundary, whose two disjoint labeled boundary faces are $(S_1\cap\Omega_{J_1})/J_1$ and $(S_2\cap\Omega_{J_2})/J_2$. Its interior is $A_0\cap\Omega_{G_0}$ modulo $G_0$. Identify these faces by the map induced by $f$. The resulting surface, with the local welding charts inherited from the sphere, is canonically biholomorphic to $\Omega_G/G$. This includes empty boundary faces and empty discontinuity quotients.

If supplied a maximal fundamental set $D_0\subset\Omega_{G_0}$—one representative of each $G_0$ orbit, with $D_0\cap B_i$ representing every $J_i$ orbit in $B_i\cap\Omega_{J_i}$ and $f(D_0\cap S_1)=D_0\cap S_2$—then
$$D=D_0\cap\bigl((\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus(B_1\cup B_2))\cup S_1\bigr)$$
is a fundamental set of $G$ on $\Omega_G$. No smooth-sided constrained-domain conclusion is implicit for arbitrary Jordan seams.

actual_proof_anchors.quote: We record the matrix convergence facts used below. For any distinct sequence $h_n$ in a discrete subgroup, choose determinant-one lifts and divide by their Euclidean matrix norms. After subsequence these converge to a nonzero singular matrix $A$: an invertible limit would bound the original norms and produce a convergent sequence of distinct elements, contradicting discreteness. The singular matrix has rank one. Its kernel line $b$ and image line $a$ give $h_n\to a$ uniformly on compact subsets of the sphere minus $b$, directly by division in homogeneous coordinates. The Hermitian formula gives $h_n o\to a$ and $h_n^{-1}o\to b$ for any model point $o$, so $a,b\in\Lambda_H$. Conversely every point of $\Lambda_H$ is such an attracting limit by choosing its orbit sequence. This also proves properness on $\Omega_H$: if infinitely many distinct $h_n$ take points of a compact $K\subset\Omega_H$ back into $K$, uniform convergence off $b\notin K$ puts their images near $a\notin K$, a contradiction. A point with a precisely invariant open neighborhood under the trivial group is not in $\Lambda_H$, since an attracting sequence sends two distinct points of that neighborhood, at least one different from $b$, back into it, contradicting precise invariance. A nonidentity element fixing a point of $\Omega_H$ would, by [F4], have that point in its limit set; thus the action there is free. These arguments apply also when $H$ is elementary. [A1, F4, F5, given, construct, algebra]

Preservation of $B_i$ also preserves its complementary closed disc. Apply step 1.1 to any attracting sequence in $J_i$, choosing one point in each disc interior different from its exceptional point. The attracting limit lies in both closed discs and hence in $S_i$. Thus $\Lambda_{J_i}\subset S_i$. The block equality now gives $B_i\cap\Lambda_{G_0}=\Lambda_{J_i}$ and $U_i\subset\Omega_{G_0}$. Joint precise invariance of regular parts gives joint open precise invariance and says that distinct discs in the family $\{gB_i:g\in G_0,i=1,2\}$ meet only on their boundaries, with every contact in $\Lambda_{G_0}$. Distinct means the same label modulo $J_i$, or different labels; equal discs with different labels are excluded by open joint invariance. The supplier [F1] applies and gives discrete torsion-free $G$ and its HNN normal forms. Apply [F2] to $S_i$ in ambient $G_0$. The distinct coset boundary curves are null. The corresponding discs are null as well: when a Jordan curve lies in a spherical ball of radius $r<\pi/4$, one complementary disc lies in that ball and the other contains its connected exterior. The latter is the only large-disc possibility. Pairwise disjoint disc interiors allow at most one such disc in any sequence with boundary diameters tending to zero. Indeed two such large discs, each containing the exterior of a ball of radius tending to zero, have intersecting interiors. Thus their diameters tend to zero. This family of closed discs is locally finite on $\Omega_{G_0}$. Otherwise distinct discs would approach a point $x$ there; their diameters tend to zero, so images of any fixed two distinct points of the appropriate $B_i$ tend to $x$. Step 1.1 forces $x$ to be the attracting limit of a subsequence, hence to lie in $\Lambda_{G_0}$, a contradiction. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

Construct the tree explicitly, rather than importing a combination-tree theorem. Its vertices are $G/G_0$. Its oriented edges are $G/J_1$, with the edge $gJ_1$ joining $gG_0$ to $gf^{-1}G_0$. This is well-defined by $fJ_1f^{-1}=J_2$. Words make the graph connected. A path with no immediate edge reversal spells a Britton-reduced word: at a reversal of stable-letter signs, equality of the two edges is exactly the condition that the intervening coefficient lies in the subgroup giving a pin. A closed nonbacktracking path would therefore give a positive-stable-length reduced word in $G_0$, which [F1] excludes by multiplying by that base element's inverse. Thus the graph is a tree $T$. The exponent homomorphism $G\to\mathbb Z$, zero on $G_0$ and one on $f$, assigns a height to every vertex. The action preserves the orientation of every edge, so has no edge inversions. At $v=G_0$, the outgoing discs for its incident edges are exactly $hB_1,hB_2$, indexed by $hJ_1,hJ_2$ respectively. Their boundary wall is the associated $hS_i$. For an edge joining $v$ to $w$, write $D(v,e)$ for its disc on the side toward $w$. The opposite disc is $D(w,e)=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\operatorname{int}D(v,e)$: at the initial edge this is precisely $f^{-1}B_2=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus U_1$. Equivariance gives this equality at every edge. [F1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

At a vertex, distinct outgoing discs have disjoint interiors and their boundary contacts lie in the corresponding conjugate of $\Lambda_{G_0}$. Along a nonbacktracking path the forward closed discs decrease: at the next vertex the next outgoing disc avoids the interior of the backward disc, so lies in its closed complement, the preceding forward disc. The inclusion at each turn is strict. The translated proper gap at that vertex lies in the interior of the preceding forward disc and outside the next closed disc. In particular successive forward discs cannot have the same boundary. No two different edges anywhere in $T$ have the same wall: orient the finite path between them forward; equality of its first and last walls would make their nested forward discs equal, or complementary, both impossible by the strict inclusion just proved. The stabilizer of the initial wall $S_1$ is consequently exactly the edge stabilizer $J_1$; that of $S_2=fS_1$ is $J_2$. For any two edges, their walls are contained in a single closed side of each other, by following their finite connecting path and the same nesting argument. This proves precise embedding, with boundary contacts allowed. Put $R_v=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\bigcup_{e\ni v}\operatorname{int}D(v,e)$ and $\Omega_v=g\Omega_{G_0}$ for $v=gG_0$. All incident walls lie in $R_v$. For $u\ne v$, the set $R_u$ lies in the closed outgoing disc for the first edge of the path from $v$ to $u$; this follows successively by taking complements of backward open discs along that path. [F1, step 3.1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

Call $Q_v=R_v\cap\Omega_v$ the regular cell. A point $x\in Q_v$ lies on at most one wall at $v$, because distinct walls contact only in $\Lambda_v$. If it lies on none, it belongs to no other $R_u$: step 4.1 would force it onto the first wall. If it lies on the wall for the edge $[v,w]$, it also lies in $Q_w$. At the initial edge this follows from $S_1\cap\Omega_{G_0}=S_1\cap\Omega_{J_1}$ and $f(S_1\cap\Omega_{J_1})=S_2\cap\Omega_{J_2}$; translate this identity for other edges. It belongs to no third $R_u$. A further edge at $w$ would force it onto a second incident wall there, contrary to $x\in\Omega_w$. Hence the set of vertices whose closed cells contain $x$ is exactly $\{v\}$ or $\{v,w\}$ as described. Local finiteness from step 2.1 supplies a neighborhood $N$ of $x$, with compact closure in each $\Omega_u$ for these one or two vertices, avoiding every outgoing closed disc at these vertices except their one common edge. Then every point of $N$ lies in at least one of their regular cells and no other closed cell. Off the edge, the two sides lie in the two respective cells; on the edge both occur. This proves the assertion for all points of $N$, not just for $x$. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

These neighborhoods prove $Q_v\subset\Omega_G$ without assuming the new block or a global null-wall conclusion. Let $K$ be the one- or two-vertex set in step 5.1. If $hN\cap N
e\varnothing$, the exact closed-cell membership of its intersection point shows $hK\cap K
e\varnothing$. Choose vertex representatives $g_uG_0=u$ for $u\in K$. Thus $h$ lies in one of the finitely many sets $g_uG_0g_t^{-1}$, $u,t\in K$. In such a set, the intersection condition implies that a $G_0$ translate of the compact set $g_t^{-1}\overline N\subset\Omega_{G_0}$ meets $g_u^{-1}\overline N\subset\Omega_{G_0}$. Properness from step 1.1 allows only finitely many such coefficients. Hence only finitely many $h$ meet $N$. An element fixing $x$ preserves its one-vertex or one-edge cell set; no edge inversion is possible by step 3.1, so it fixes a vertex and belongs to its conjugate of $G_0$. Freeness on $\Omega_v$ from step 1.1 makes it identity. Shrink $N$ to exclude the finite remaining nonidentity translates. It is then precisely invariant under identity; step 1.1 implies $x
otin\Lambda_G$. This proves the claimed inclusion with a genuine open-neighborhood argument at arbitrary Jordan seams. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

Each point of $S_i\setminus\Lambda_{J_i}$ lies in the regular cell at its incident vertex, by step 2.1, so step 6.1 places it in $\Omega_G$. The reverse inclusion of limit sets $\Lambda_{J_i}\subset\Lambda_G$ is immediate from orbit inclusions. Consequently $S_i\cap\Lambda_G=\Lambda_{J_i}$. If a translate takes a point of $S_i\cap\Omega_G$ back to this set, it takes its exact incident edge of step 5.1 to the same edge, so belongs to its stabilizer $J_i$. This gives precise invariance. Boundary clearance is the unchanged given condition on $S_i$ and $J_i$. We may now, and only now, apply [F2] in ambient $G$ to $S_1$: all its hypotheses, including its ambient limit-set intersection, have been proved. Distinct edge walls are distinct coset translates by step 4.1, so their spherical diameters tend to zero. Since $S_2=fS_1$, this is the assertion for either boundary and the whole edge-wall family. Along any infinite nonbacktracking tree ray its nested forward discs also have diameters tending to zero. Once their boundaries are sufficiently small, a large complementary disc would contain the exterior of an arbitrarily small spherical ball. This cannot persist inside the first fixed proper closed disc, whose complement contains a fixed nonempty open ball. Hence only the small-side alternative remains. Compact nested discs therefore intersect in one point. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, given, algebra]

At $v_0=G_0$ the regular cell is exactly the $Q$ of the Statement. Indeed a point outside all open discs either lies outside all their closed discs, or on at least one translated boundary. Thus $$Q=(A_0\cup G_0(S_1\cup S_2))\cap\Omega_{G_0}.$$ At its regular boundary points exactly one incident disc occurs, and the local neighborhoods of step 5.1 identify $Q$ with its closed side of a Jordan curve. At its other points it is open in the sphere. Consequently it is a topological surface with boundary. For completeness [F7] supplies closed-disc parametrizations of both sides. Their boundary parametrizations differ by a circle homeomorphism, which extends radially by $r\zeta\mapsto r h(\zeta)$ to the closed disc. Correct one parametrization by this extension and glue the two matching parametrizations. The resulting continuous bijection from the sphere to itself is a homeomorphism by compactness and the Hausdorff property, and sends the equator to the seam. Restricting it gives the needed local half-disc charts. No differentiability of the Jordan boundary is used. The free proper $G_0$ action gives the same local description of $Q/G_0$. Joint precise invariance identifies its boundary exactly as the disjoint labeled quotients of $S_1\cap\Omega_{J_1}$ and $S_2\cap\Omega_{J_2}$. Its interior is exactly $(A_0\cap\Omega_{G_0})/G_0$, including the possible empty case. [F1, F7, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

Suppose $x$ lies neither in a regular cell nor in a translate of $\Lambda_{G_0}$. Starting at any vertex, $x$ then lies in exactly one outgoing open disc: failure to lie in any would put it in that regular cell. Move to its next vertex. The next choice cannot be the backward edge, whose open disc is disjoint from the preceding forward open disc. This constructs an infinite tree ray, with $x$ in the interior of every nested forward disc. Step 7.1 makes their diameters tend to zero. After each chosen edge, choose a later wall whose whole closed disc lies inside the previous open disc; this is possible because the discs shrink to $x$, which is in that open disc. The chosen walls are pairwise disjoint and nest about $x$. Their group representatives are distinct, and their walls converge to $x$. Apply step 1.1 to those representatives and choose two distinct fixed points of $S_1$; their images both approach $x$, so the attracting limit is $x$. Thus $x\in\Lambda_G$. In particular no point of $\Omega_G$ can fail to belong to some $Q_v$: it belongs to every $\Omega_v$, and the preceding argument would make it a limit point. We have proved $\Omega_G=\bigcup_{v\in T}Q_v$. Conversely if $x\in\Lambda_G\setminus\bigcup_v\Lambda_v$, step 6.1 prevents membership in a regular cell and the construction proves the required nesting. [F1, step 1.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

Let $h$ not be conjugate into $G_0$. By [F6] choose a positive-length cyclically reduced representative of a conjugate of $h$. The path from the base vertex spelled by this representative and all its translates by its positive and negative powers concatenate without reversals, because there is no interior pin or end pin. They form a bi-infinite tree path on which $h$ translates. Along its two directions step 7.1 gives shrinking closed discs and hence fixed limit points $p_+,p_-$ of $h$ on the sphere. They lie in the opposite closed discs of every edge on this path. By [F4], $h$ is loxodromic or parabolic. In the parabolic case its unique fixed point $p$ equals both $p_+$ and $p_-$ and hence lies on an axis wall. Conjugate that wall to $S_1$. Step 7.1 puts $p$ in $\Lambda_{J_1}$. This point cannot be conical for $J_1$. To justify the needed ambient exclusion explicitly, a translation $T_\ell$ fixing a parabolic point has the complex Shimizu bound $|\ell c|\ge1$ for all ambient matrices with $c\ne0$. If it failed, after scaling $\ell=1$ the iterates $a_{n+1}=1-a_nc_n$, $c_{n+1}=-c_n^2$, $b_{n+1}=a_n^2$, $d_{n+1}=1+a_nc_n$ of $g_{n+1}=g_nT_1g_n^{-1}$ would have $c_n\to0$, bounded $a_n\to1$, and distinct matrices converging to $T_1$, contradicting discreteness. Formula [F5] now bounds the height of every ambient orbit point by $\max(Y_0,\ell^2/Y_0)$; elements with $c=0$ belong to the full parabolic translation stabilizer of [F4] and keep height $Y_0$. A conical orbit tending to this point infinity within bounded distance of its vertical ray would have unbounded height, impossible. Thus no subgroup can have that point conical. For nonelementary $J_1$, [F3] makes $p$ parabolic. For elementary $J_1$, a finite limit set of size at least three makes the group finite: the permutation kernel fixes three points and is trivial. Torsion-freeness then makes it trivial. An empty limit set also forces triviality since every nonidentity element has ideal orbit limits. If there are two limit points, an interchange has order two and is excluded. The group fixes both, is diagonal and cyclic: multipliers in a compact annulus form a finite set by discreteness, so their nonzero logarithmic absolute values have a least positive value and no modulus-one kernel. Its two endpoints are conical along its axis, and are excluded here. A one-point limit set forces every element to fix that point, with no loxodromic element, and [F4] gives a translation group. Hence here too $p$ is parabolic for $J_1$. This proves the full nonloxodromic classification while allowing the full ambient stabilizer to have larger rank. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

A nesting sequence cannot converge to an old vertex limit point. Fix a vertex $v$. Its closed cell $R_v$ contains an incident Jordan wall and hence two distinct points $a,b$. For any edge, its closed half-disc toward $v$ contains all of $R_v$, by the path containment in step 4.1. In a sequence nesting about $x$, the closed sides containing $x$ eventually have diameters tending to zero: the boundaries do, and the nested small-side argument of step 7.1 applies after fixing its first proper side. They cannot then be the sides toward $v$, which contain both $a,b$. For all sufficiently late terms they are the sides away from $v$, contained in one of the outgoing closed discs at $v$. Since $x$ is in the interior of each such side, it is in the interior of that outgoing disc. But every such interior lies in $\Omega_v$, by step 2.1 and equivariance. Therefore $x\notin\Lambda_v$. As $v$ was arbitrary this excludes all old translates. The same two-point attracting argument of step 8.1 shows any nesting limit lies in $\Lambda_G$. This completes both directions of the precise nested-limit-set characterization. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra]

The natural map from $Q$ to $\Omega_G/G$ is surjective after quotienting by $G_0$, by step 8.1 and equivariance of cells. Its exact identifications are the stated side pairing. If $x,y\in Q$ and $hx=y$, the vertex $v_0$ and $hv_0$ both occur in the exact cell set of $y$. They are either equal, giving $h\in G_0$, or are the endpoints of its one incident edge, giving a seam identification. Transitivity of $G_0$ on each of its two incident edge types reduces this identification to $f:S_1\cap\Omega_{J_1}\to S_2\cap\Omega_{J_2}$ or its inverse. There are no other identifications and no transitive chains through a third face, because each regular cell set has at most two vertices. The local patch $N$ of step 5.1, shrunk precisely invariant as in step 6.1, proves that this bijection is a homeomorphism in the quotient topologies: away from seams it is the usual open-cell chart, and across a seam it is precisely the two closed halves of $N$ identified along their common Jordan arc. These charts also define its conformal structure. On one half use the identity sphere coordinate; on the other use the inverse of the given Möbius side-pairing after bringing that cell to the first vertex. The seam chart is the single open sphere patch $N$. Two such charts have transition a restriction of a group Möbius transformation, also across their seams, because they are restrictions of quotient charts for the free properly discontinuous $G$ action. They are holomorphic. The homeomorphism is therefore biholomorphic for this explicit welding atlas. This proves conformal gluing without either simply connected component hypotheses or smooth seam assumptions. [F1, F5, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 8.1, step 7.2, construct, algebra]

Finally assume the supplied maximal $D_0$. Write $A=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus(B_1\cup B_2)$. We have $D_0\cap A=D_0\cap A_0$. For if $x\in D_0\cap A$ lies in $gB_i$, then $g^{-1}x\in B_i\cap\Omega_{G_0}$ has a $J_i$ translate $z\in D_0\cap B_i$ by maximality. Since $x,z$ are two representatives of the same base orbit, they are equal, contrary to $x\in A$. Conversely $A_0\subset A$. Every interior orbit of the cut-space is thus represented exactly once by $D_0\cap A$. Each of its two labeled boundary orbits is represented exactly once by $D_0\cap S_i$, and maximality pairs these representatives by $f$. Removing the second face and retaining the first therefore gives exactly one representative of every glued orbit, precisely the displayed $D$. By step 9.2 these are exactly the $G$ orbits in $\Omega_G$, so $D$ is the asserted fundamental set. Nothing here asserts smooth sides for the arbitrary Jordan seams or boundedness of every new parabolic point. [F1, step 7.2, step 9.2, given, algebra] ∎

actual_reading_notes:
The actual complete Space II article was read, all 22 pages, from `/tmp/kt72-maskit-space-ii-authentic.txt` and its actual published PDF, SHA256 5a067d9a2b712dccfdb548519bdba8782c7bbcc2ffc37b12045abda3c70a26fd. The repository-hosted published Space I PDF has a repository cover and 45 article pages, SHA256 9a90e6bb93ea5d579c5a2cb62fdb2341539e4542a3ae4d9f03ee63c962b0b873. Its entire Sections 3–4 were read from the pagewise OCR, PDF pp. 14–39, together with its Section 2.2 definitions; other pages are not claimed here. The actual current HNN algebraic, null-coset, cyclic reduction and Jordan-boundary suppliers were read in full. The previously authored local-thin, conical criterion and hyperbolic model proofs were read in full in their development.

Space II explicitly omits proofs of Theorem 3.1(1)–(8) as similar to other works. None of those omissions supplies a proof here. Its literal clause (8) omits the second face from its displayed cut-space and writes the unglued quotient as the final quotient; the precise two-face welding construction above states the actual intended operation. Space I Definition 2.2 requires smooth sides for a constrained fundamental domain. Arbitrary Jordan seams, even with the stated finite measure-zero intersection with old side frontiers, do not by themselves supply smooth new sides. That optional smooth-sided conclusion is therefore not asserted. The full fundamental-set, regular translated-boundary, new-parabolic, nested-limit and conformal-gluing conclusions are proved above with contacts retained. Torsionful orbifold extensions and the bounded-parabolic/conical conditions needed for full output geometrical finiteness remain separate obligations; no general hyperbolization completion is claimed.
